name: Rebar
seoDesc: Rebar: work out rebar pieces rows from the length and the width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Rebar calculator turns the length, the width and more into rebar pieces rows. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Rebar calculator work?
sections.html:
The Rebar calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports rebar pieces rows in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the length, the width, the rebar price and the price of a single rebar.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Rebar calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Edge-grid=-1 ÷ 2 × grid length + (1 ÷ 2) × length
Edge-grid=-1 ÷ 2 × grid width + (1 ÷ 2) × width
Total cost of rebars=price of a single rebar × rounded up, ((grid length × rounded up, ((grid width + rebar-rebar (grid)) ÷ rebar-rebar (grid)) + grid width × rounded up, ((grid length + rebar-rebar (grid)) ÷ rebar-rebar (grid))) ÷ length of a single rebar)
Length of a single rebar=price of a single rebar ÷ rebar price
Rebar pieces rows=rounded up, ((grid length + rebar-rebar (grid)) ÷ rebar-rebar (grid))
Rebar pieces columns=rounded up, ((grid width + rebar-rebar (grid)) ÷ rebar-rebar (grid))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Rebar-rebar (grid) = 40 cm, Edge-grid = 8 cm, Rebar price = 2 and Length of a single rebar = 600 m — it reports Price of a single rebar = 12.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Price of a single rebar = 12 should be roughly the size you expected from Rebar-rebar (grid) = 40 cm and Edge-grid = 8 cm.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Rebar calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length, the width and the rebar price — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Rebar calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns rebar pieces rows, derived from the length, the width and the rebar price. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Rebar calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the width, the rebar price and the price of a single rebar, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Price of a single rebar = 12. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Rebar calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
